name: Advanced desalination and water reuse
summary: Advanced membranes, energy recovery, treatment controls and reuse systems turn saline or previously used water into dependable supplies for cities and industry.
useCase: A water-stressed city purifies treated wastewater for replenishing drinking-water supplies, while a semiconductor plant recirculates more of its process water.
whyNow: The opportunity combines established treatment processes with better efficiency, monitoring and integration. Orange County’s Groundwater Replenishment System illustrates proven potable-reuse expansion: design capacity increased from 100 million gallons per day to 130 million in 2023. This single-site metric is deliberately kept separate from global desalination or reuse-market estimates. The World Bank’s 2025 work identifies much larger potential for industrial and potable reuse, but infrastructure investment depends on tariffs, financing, treatment reliability and customer confidence. A membrane efficiency improvement alone does not resolve brine disposal, distribution, energy supply or water quality. The practical objective is a dependable cubic metre delivered at an acceptable full-system cost.

mainstream.scope: Routine selection of advanced reuse and efficient desalination packages for suitable new projects in water-stressed cities and water-intensive industries.
mainstream.rationale: Conventional desalination and some potable reuse are already established. The emerging phase is broader reuse acceptance, higher recovery, better energy efficiency and integrated industrial water loops. Multi-year permitting and construction imply gradual adoption. Affordable alternatives, brine-management limits or weak utility finances can make the local date much later.

direction: Expanding where water scarcity supports investment

metric.name: Orange County GWRS design treatment capacity
metric.scope: One advanced potable-reuse system in California; site-level deployment proxy.

points.status: existing design capacity from operator timeline

metric.limitations: This is nameplate capacity at one facility, not its daily realised output or the size of the global reuse/desalination market. The 2021 value reflects the 100 MGD expansion completed in 2015, which remained in place until the 2023 expansion. It does not imply annual measured production.
metric.futureNote: No defensible comparable external deployment forecast found. The separate maturity path is an analyst scenario, not measured adoption.
metric.growthLabel: Representative reuse plant: 100 → 130 MGD capacity in 2023

milestones.text: GWRS operated with the 100 MGD design capacity established by its 2015 expansion; the number is a capacity baseline.
No new comparable GWRS capacity step is reported in the operator timeline; global capacity is not inferred from this one plant.
GWRS completed its final expansion to 130 MGD, a 30% increase in design capacity.
The operator’s account retains 130 MGD capacity; this is not evidence of identical daily output.
World Bank published Scaling Water Reuse, assessing potential expansion and the policy/finance needed to deliver it.
GWRS continues to state 130 MGD design capacity, while Gradiant announced new financing for industrial-water expansion in May. These are different types of evidence.

tailwinds: Water scarcity and industrial reliability needs can make diversified supply valuable.
Energy recovery, better membranes and control systems can improve operating economics.
Large industrial users can be anchor customers for well-defined reuse projects.
bottlenecks: Brine, concentrate and residuals must be managed as part of the full project.
Energy prices, financing and distribution infrastructure strongly affect delivered water cost.
Public acceptance and verified water quality are essential for potable applications.
watchMetrics: Actual cubic metres supplied and plant availability, separated from nameplate capacity.
Full delivered cost per cubic metre, including energy, chemicals, residuals and distribution.
Water recovery, energy intensity, contaminant performance and repeat municipal/industrial contracts.
